Deference: The Transformation of Auto Safety Regulation, 34 Ya l e J ON Re g

5. 
Technology Forcing in Other Contexts. While the courts helped to 
make technology-forcing regulation difficult and even impossible for NHTSA, 
they created somewhat more latitude for that approach in some other contexts, 
including EPA regulation under the Clean Air Act. An illustrative case is 
Natural Resources Defense Council v. EPA, 655 F.2d 318 (D.C. Cir. 1981), in 
which the agency promulgated rules on emissions of a major Air pollutant 
(particulate matter) from diesel trucks. In evaluating the automakers’ 
challenge under the arbitrary-or-capricious standard, the D.C. Circuit said:
In the present case, GM attacks the EPA’s estimation of the 
period of time necessary to permit the development and apphcation 
of the requisite technology” to achieve comphance with the 1985 
particulate standards. The agency has determined that the 
technology will be available in time, and now seeks to defend its 
conclusion as a product of reasoned decisionmaking. Such predictions 
inherently involve a greater degree of uncertainty than estimations 
of the effectiveness of current technology. If we judge the EPA’s action 
by the st^dard of certainty appropriate to current technology, the 
agency will be unable to set pollutant levels until the necessary 
technology is already available.
The legislative history of both the 1970 and the 1977 
amendments [to the Clean Air Act] demonstrates that Congress 
intended the agency to project future advances in pollution control 
capability. It was expected to press for the development and 
apphcation of improved technology rather than be hmited by that 
which exists today.” S.Rep.No.ll96, 91st Cong., 2d Sess. 24 (1970).
This court has upheld the agency’s power to make such 
projections, while recognizing that it is “subject to the restraints of 
reasonableness, and does not open the door to ‘crystal ball’ inquiry.” 
International Harvester Co. v. Ruckelshaus, 478 F.2d 615, 629 (D.C. 
Cir. 1973). The Clean Air Act requires the EPA to look to the future 
in setting standards, but the agency must also provide a reasoned 
explanation of its basis for beheving that its projection is reliable. 
This includes a defense of its methodology for arriving at numerical 
estimates. * * *
The tune element in the EPA’s prediction affects our reviewing 
task in three distinct ways. First, it introduces uncertainties in the 
agency’s judgment that render that judgment vulnerable to attack. 
At the same time, however, the time element gives the EPA greater 
scope for confidence that theoretical solutions will be translated 
successfully into mechanical realizations, for “the question of 
availabihty is partially dependent on lead time’, the time in which 
the technology will have to be available.” Portland Cement
